title: How Tulsa Invented the Chicken Dance by Accident - NewsBreak
text:
By Kelso ,
1 days ago
This might be one of the strangest bits of Oklahoma trivia you’ll ever hear — the story of how Oklahoma accidentally invented the Chicken Dance. It all started with a simple case of the wrong costume.
The song itself goes back decades. It was written by a Swiss composer in the 1950s, and it almost instantly became a polka classic that spread around the world through small-town festivals, and Oklahoma weddings… If you know, you know.
Think The Lawrence Welk Show kind of energy.
via GIPHY
Originally known as the “Duck Dance” across Europe, the tune made its way into Oktoberfests everywhere. The English called it “The Birdy Dance.” But when it finally reached America, specifically the Tulsa Oktoberfest, it took on an entirely new meaning.
Tulsa’s Oktoberfest Mishap Today, Tulsa’s Oktoberfest is ranked among the best German festivals in the world, just behind Munich itself. But back in 1981, it was still getting its footing. Rain soaked the festival grounds that year, and organizers weren’t sure anyone would even show up for a weekend of mud and polka.
via GIPHY
Tulsa’s local KJRH Channel 2 showed up expecting a washout story, but Oklahomans have never been scared off by bad weather. To help draw a crowd, the crew decided to broadcast some live music and dancing.
The Duck Dance was catching on at the time, so they planned to feature it. Channel 2 even offered to bring a duck costume for the bit.
When Ducks Become Chickens Someone from the station ran back to grab the old duck suit from storage, but it turned out to be a chicken costume instead.
Rather than scrap the idea, they just went for it. One brave volunteer put on the oversized chicken suit, flapped along to the music, and history was rewritten.
From that soggy afternoon at the 1981 Tulsa Oktoberfest, the Duck Dance officially became known across America as The Chicken Dance .
Only in Oklahoma could a mix-up like that turn into a nationwide tradition.

Oklahoma's Top 10 Pumpkin Patches & Corn Mazes If you're looking for a place to go for a little fall family fun, then you're in luck! Oklahoma is home to some of the biggest and best pumpkin patches and corn mazes in the nation. People from all over travel to the Sooner State every fall to visit these incredible farms. Not only do they offer pumpkin patches along with corn and hay mazes, they also have all kinds of other activities like petting zoos, rides, arts and crafts, food, games, haunted attractions, and a whole lot more. So no matter what your idea of fall fun is, you can find it all in one place! Gallery Credit: Jeri Anderson Annabell's Fun Farm Facebook Annabell's Fun Farm - Welch, Oklahoma You'll find Annabell's Fun Farm at 444584 E. 110 Road in Welch, Oklahoma. They have a pumpkin patch, corn maze and other fall family fun. For more information, go to their official website or check them out on Facebook . DaZe in a MaZe Facebook DaZe in a MaZe - Marshall, Oklahoma You'll find DaZe in a MaZe 11 miles South of Covington on Highway 74 or 2 miles North of Highway 51 & 74 Junction in Marshall, Oklahoma. If you're looking for some fall family fun head to DaZe in a MaZe. They have a corn maze, petting zoo and all kinds of other activities the entire family will enjoy. Get all the details on their official website or visit their Facebook Page for more information. Chester's Party Barn & Farm Facebook Chester's Party Barn & Farm - Piedmont, Oklahoma You'll find Chester's Party Barn & Farm at 5201 Cimarron Road NW in Piedmont, Oklahoma. They have a pumpkin patch, petting zoo, pony rides, and all kinds of other great fall family fun. Get all the details on their official website or visit their Facebook Page for more information. Brown Ranch Hay Maze Facebook Brown Ranch Hay Maze - Ardmore, Oklahoma Located at US Highway South 77 Campbell Street in Ardmore, Oklahoma the Brown Ranch hay maze has one of the largest hay mazes in Oklahoma and all kinds of fall family fun. From hayrides to hay mazes and more. For details, visit their official website or check them out on Facebook . Livesay Orchards Facebook Livesay Orchards - Porter, Oklahoma Check out Livesay Orchards located at 39232 E. 231 Street in Porter, Oklahoma. Probably best known for their peaches, but they also have a pumpkin patch and other fall fun the entire family will enjoy. For details, visit their official website or check them out on Facebook . Orr Family Farm Facebook Orr Family Farm - Oklahoma City, Oklahoma This place has it all including Cannon Blasters and Zombie Apocalypse Paintball! The Orr Family Farm is located at 14400 S. Western Avenue in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. They have a fall maze, petting zoo, train rides, and more. Go to the official website for details or visit them on Facebook . Parkhurst Pumpkin Patch Facebook Parkhurst Pumpkin Patch - Arcadia, Oklahoma The Parkhurst Pumpkin Patch is located at 720 S. Henney Road in Arcadia, Oklahoma. They have a corn and hay maze you can explore along with pony rides, a petting zoo, picnic areas, hay forts, and hayrides. Get all the details by visiting their official website or their Facebook page . Sunshine Shelly's Pumpkin Patch Facebook Sunshine Shelly's Pumpkin Patch - Shawnee, Oklahoma You'll find Sunshine Shelly's Pumpkin Patch at 7110 N. Harrison in Shawnee, Oklahoma. They have a huge corn maze, hayrides, corn pits, a kiddie maze, and a fifteen-acre pumpkin patch where you can pick your own pumpkin. Check them out on Facebook . Sweet Pickins Pumpkin Patch Facebook Sweet Pickins Pumpkin Patch - Altus Sweet Pickins Pumpkin Patch is located just north of Altus, Oklahoma at 15830 S County Road. The farm features a pumpkin patch, fall family games, petting zoo, photo ops and more! Check them out on Facebook . Bigfoot Ranch Pumpkin Patch Facebook Bigfoot Ranch Pumpkin Patch Bigfoot Ranch Pumpkin Patch is located at 16731 NW Madische Road in Apache, Oklahoma. The ranch offers a pumpkin patch, fall activities, hay rides, maze and photo ops with Bigfoot! Check them out on Facebook . Where To See Fall Colors In Oklahoma Whether it's the feeling you get when you see falls warm colors in the trees, or the comfort of a memory you recall from a younger time in your life, there are places in Oklahoma to see the beauty of autumn. Gallery Credit: Kelso lilkar 14. The Wichita Mountains While a leisurely drive through the Wichita's might not offer you the best and most scenic fall foliage, getting off the beaten path is where this place comes alive. It's not so much the trees that take on falls color, it's the shrubs and lesser vegetation. Christopher Mills 13. Roman Nose State Park The clear water springs that flow through this park, replenishing the hardwoods that have rooted a home, the true beauty of this place is seeing the red bluffs in the low fall sunlight. Best experienced near sunset. winyuu 12. Red Rock Adventure Park While not much to look at as November rolls on, this is the place in Oklahoma you can normally see the earliest changing of the foliage. This park of canyons offers stunning views of vibrant red maples backed by red sandstone walls. Best seen the last week of October into the first few days of November. Gerald G Gantar 11. Osage Hills State Park Whether it's the rolling hills and meadows or the gradients of changing trees, Osage Hills is a great place to see foliage from the car. It's expected to turn around Halloween and really pop the first two weeks of November. Chad Elberson 10. Oologah Reservior The states most majestic forest of oak and hickory trees can be found around Oologah Lake in Northeastern Oklahoma. Famed for being the birth place of Will Rogers and unparalleled hiking trails like Skull Hollow, the colors of fall are primed to burst forth any day now. Prime season is the first two weeks of November. ShriramPatki 9. Lake Murray State Park It's only natural that Oklahoma's largest state park land somewhere on this list. Normally it's the fishing, golf, and camping that attract people to this place, but three weeks each year, it's the foliage. Peaking the last week of October through mid-November on average. Take a drive along Hickory Creek for the best in-vehicle views. Holcy 8. Great Salt Plains State Park Most people know this place for the great salt plain that stretches as far as you can see here... but as the foliage turns into yellows and oranges, the white salt backdrop offers a very unique view. Peaking last week of October through the first week of November. DavidPrahl 7. Boiling Springs State Park You wouldn't expect to find fall colors in a veritable desert, but the scenic trail between Woodward and the Alabaster Caverns offers a unique view. Towering hardwoods taking on fall colors amid the sandy sagebrush covered hills. It's a rarity worth exploring. Best seen the last week of October and the first week of November. ejesposito 6. Miami to Tahlequah If you find yourself in Miami (pronounced My-am-uh) Oklahoma this time of year and you're looking for the best fall views, take State Highway 10 and soak in the autumn views all the way to Tahlequah. It's one of the most heavily forested portions of the state. Colors peak the last week of October through the first two weeks of November. lauraag 5. Tahlequah to Sallisaw Since you're already there, you might as well hop onto Hwy 51 and head towards Sallisaw. The views continue all the way down US Hwy 59. Colors peak last week of October through the second week of November. helivideo 4. Chickasaw National Recreation Area Oklahoma's original national park, the Chickasaw National Recreation Area offers some of the most beautiful sweeping views in the state. Drive through the various campgrounds and experience being in the color-changing canopy. Best seen the last week of October through the first week of November. 3. Robbers Cave State Park The Southeastern part of Oklahoma is the true jewel of fall foliage, and Robbers Cave is the perfect introduction. Tucked away in a hidden area, State Highway 2 will guide you through some terrific views. Best colors pop last week of October and first week of November. 2. Kiamichi Trace Stretching from the banks of the Red River along the OK/TX border and flowing North of Fort Smith along the Arkansas border, the Kiamichi Trace is arguably the prettiest place to see fall foliage in Oklahoma. Others disagree and suggest the #1 spot on this list earned it. Either/or, you can see both in the same day. Best viewed the last week of October through the first week of November. leekris 1. Talimena National Scenic Byway If you want to experience every gradient of falls color all in once place, there is no better road to travel than the Talimena National Scenic Byway. State Highway 1 will take you through the twists and turns of the Quachita Mountains, offering secluded comforts and spanning vistas of natures beauty. Best views can be found the last weekend in October and the first week of November. 2
